against itself, can never stand. I am not apportioning blame for whatever 
reason it happened; it happened. The pe ople of India have given their verdict.

enforcement, ...(Time-bell)... the question of

Sir, when we talk of security, we talk of food security, we talk of

I do want to make a few points with respect to what Mr. Arun Shourie 
stated in his intervention. He made three points. In reference to the 
amendment of POTA, he said, 'Don't ferment a permissive environment'. 
Perhaps many of my colleagues and friends don't know that my Ph.D. has 
been in the legal control of the international terrorism. I have a little theoretical 
knowledge of security issues, and, I co me from the State of Punjab where we 
experimented with TADA. Sir, if today, we  are rid of terrorism in Punjab, it is 
not because of TADA, and if today, we have failed to eliminate terrorism in 
other parts of the country, it is not because of POTA being there on the 
Statute book. Everyone knows that oppre ssive laws ferment dissatisfaction, 
they breed violence, they compel people to resort to extra-constitutional and

Therefore, my answer to my esteemed friend, Mr. Arun Shourie would be that 
the elimination of oppressive laws is a step forward in securing our internal

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER (MAHARASHTRA): Madam Vice-Chairman, I 
would like to begin with a few observations about our general attitude to 
internal security. As a nation, we have been attaching comparatively less 
importance to problems relevant to internal security than to external security. 
Somehow or the other, a philosophy seems to have developed among our 
people that once we have shaken off the foreign yoke and asserted our right 
to be our own masters in our own houses, sovereignty will automatically be 
preserved, security will automatically be part of the element of sovereignty; 
and, therefore, we are treating internal secu rity as if it is only a law and order 
problem. Confusing law and order with in ternal security has been the greatest 
weakness in our approach to internal security problems. That is my first point.

what has happend to various nations in the post-world War period, we should 
really be much more concerned on the problem of internal security than what 
we are today.

Drug research in India 
*221. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY. Will the Minister of 
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) what steps his Ministry is taking or propose to take to focus on drug 
research in India; 
(b) the money spent on drug research during the last five years, year-wise; 
(c) the money spent on drug research, percentage-wise, out of profit earned 
by companies during the last five years, year-wise; and 
(d) the measures Government are taking to make India a leader in drug 
development? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPILSIBAL): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Ministry of Science and Technology is taking several steps and 
measures to focus on drug research  to make India a leader in drug 
development. Some of these steps and measures are: 
increasing the outlay for Research and Development (R&D) on drug 
research 

RAJYASABHA [16 December, 2004J 
introducing newer programmes for drugs and pharmaceuticals R&D' 
encouraging collaborative R&D projects among laboratories/ 
institutions/industry in modern and Indian Systems of Medicine i.e. 
public-private partnership 
establishing state-of-the-art facilities 
strengthening the human resource development through research 
fellowships, young scientist scheme, etc. 
establishment of Pham iaceutical Research a nd Development Support 
fund(PRDSF) 
the Technology Development Boar(i of DST is supporting research and 
commercialization in the private sector, with, good results, and 
organising Pharma Industry-Institutional interactive meet, seminar, 
symposia on modern, ayurveda, unani, siddha systems of medicine 
including veterinary drug development. 
(b) During the last five years Ministry of Science and Technology has spent 
Rs.5143 lakhs in 1999-2000, Rs.4187 lakhs in 2000-01, Rs. 4948 lakhs in 
2001-02, R8.6340 lakhs in 2002-03 and Rs. 8910 lakhs in 2003-04 respectively 
on drug research.

(d) As provided in part (a) of the question above.

Facilities to Gramin Dak Sevaks 
*235. SHRl C. RAMACHANDRAI AH: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether three lakh Gramin Dak Sevaks maintaining communications 
services to rural Indian are being deni ed all facilities and benefits despite 
Supreme Court's ruling to treat them as holders of civilian posts; 
(b) the details of their pending demands; and 
(c) the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRl DAYANIDHI MARAN): (a) The Hon'ble Supreme 
Court, in the case of RK. Rajamma, 1977 (3) SCC 1994, has held that 
although an Extra Departmental Ag ent (EDA), now called Gramin Dak 
Sevak (GDS) holds a civil post under the administrative control of the State, 
such a post is outside the regular Civil Services. The EDAs now 
43 

RAJYASABHA [16 December, 2004] 
called Gramin Dak Sevaks, therefore, do  not form part of the regular Civil 
Services as they are not regular Government employees, but a class apart. They are 
part-time employees employed for a period upto a maximum of 5 hours per day 
Consequent upon the recommendations of the Justice Talwar Committee, the 
issue of grant of status of regular Govt, employees to the Gramin Dak Sevaks was 
examined by the Group of Ministers (GoM) and thereafter by the Government in 
1998, but not accepted. Subsequently while examining the issue of change of 
nomenclature of the Extra Departmental Agents, the matter was again 
considered by the Group of Ministers and thereafter by the Govemment in 
December, 2000 but rejected. As such Gramin Dak Sevaks are not eligible for all 
benefits and facilities which are admissible to the regular Government 
employees. Their terms and conditions of employment are governed by a 
separate set of rules called Gramin Dak Sevaks Conduct & Employment 
Rules, 2001. 
(b) The Gramin Dak Sevaks have been making demands, the major ones 
being grant of status, for grant of pension (Social Security), maternity leave for 
women GDSs, all trade union facilities for the office bearers of their union & 
merger of 50% Dearness Allowance w ith the Time Related Continuity 
Allowance. 
(c) The reaction of the Govt, on the above issues is as below: 
Demand for grant of pension/social security: While examining the 
recommendations of Justice Talw ar Committee set up in 1985, the 
Government did not find the demand for grant of pension feasible. However, a new 
element viz. SeveranceAmountof Rs. 20,000/-or 30,000/-depending on the period 
of employment has been introduced w.e.f. 17.12.1998. 
Demand for grant of maternity leave: The recommendation of the Justice 
Talwar Committee for grant of leave including maternity leave was considered by 
the Government. However, paid leave at the rate of 10 days for each half year 
without the facility of carry forward or encashment was accepted. Further 
Gramin Dak Sevaks can avail leave without allowances upto maximum of 180 
days in a year. 
Demand for grant of all trade union facilities: The All India Postal Extra 
Departmental Employees Union has already been availing of a number of trade union 
facilities. However, their demand forgrantof facility of Foreign Service and Special 
Casual Leave was considered by the Government, but not accepted due to the 
reasons that these are available only to  the Associations/Unions of regular 
Government servants. 
44 

[16 December, 2004] RAJYASABHA 
Demand for Merger of 50% Dearne ss Allowance (DA) with Time 
Related Continuity Allowance (TRCA) of Gramin Dak Sevaks: The 
Government had allowed Time Related Continuity Allowance (TRCA) of 
Gramin Dak Sevaks: as full and final se ttlement of Justice Talwar Committee 
recommendations and Cabinet had approved merger of DA only for regular Central 
Government employees. Therefore, the benefit of merger of 50% DA with 
TRCA has not been extended to the GDSs who are outside the regular Civil 
Service.

500 population in an individual village or 1000 population in a group of villages.

(a) In Normal Areas:

(b) In Hilly, Tribal, Desert and Inaccessible Areas:

distance limit can be relaxed by tHe Directorate in cases where such relaxation is 
warranted by special circumstances which should be clearly explained while 
submitting a proposal.

It is further to be ensured that as a result of opening of new post office, the loss in 
respect of parent'post office does not increase beyond the permissible limit nor is its 
income reduced below the minimum prescribed.

new Central Government recruits (excluding Armed Forces, in the first stage) with effect

Allowance to be paid by the employee and matched by the Central Government. The New

1552. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of SCIENCE

(a) whether it is a fact that CCMB, Hyderabad has discovered a new

174 

[16 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, what is the new technique that has been discovered by the

(c) in what manner, it helps in catching the poachers of animals? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The new technique uses a pair of novel primers which can amplify by the 
polymerase chain reaction the genetic ma terial from a biological tissue. The 
amplified DNA is sequenced and in-silico analysis is carried out using global 
database. This enables us to establish the identity of the biological sample with 
respect of the species it has been derived from. 
(c) This technique helps in catching the poachers of the animals by not only 
establishing the identity of the animal, but also indirectly identifying and 
linking the poacher to the crime as sometimes odd bits of carcass and chunks 
of meat are the only thing found in the possession of the poacher, thus making 
it difficult to positively identify the pa rticular animal poached. Using this 
technique more than 50 cases, fonwarded by various wildlife curators and crime 
investigation agencies have been resolved.

SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE:

 laws, pertaining to minimum wages, right to form union etc. and workers

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) There have been no reports of any violation of any Labour Laws 
pertaining to minimum wages, right to form Union or any anti workers activities by 
the Contractor Messrs Hindustan Construction Company (HCC) engaged in 
construction work in Banihal. In so far as compliance of the provisions of 
Minimum Wages Act is concerned, it is to inform that wages

Construction Company Workers Union, Banihal. This Union is affiliated to

*245. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that according to a study jointly carried out by 
AIIMS and World Bank, 69 per cent of the injections given at Government 
hospitals are unsafe and contribute in spreading diseases like AIDS, Hepatitis 
and Malaria; 
(b) if so, the other revelations made by the above study; and 
(c) the action that has been contemplated by Government on the 
outcome of the study? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
The assessment of injection practices in India was carried out by India 
CLEN programme Evaluation Network under Clinical Epidemiology unit under 
AIIMS, New Delhi. The study was funded by the World Bank. The draft report 
has been submitted to the Ministry. The final report is still awaited. One of the 
findings in the draft report is that 35% of injections given at Government 
hospitals are unsafe because of improper sterilization, whereas another 34% of 
injections are unsafe because of wrong injection habits of the injection givers. 
22 

[17 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
Some of the other important findings in the above study are as 
follows:— 
(i) Approximately 300 crore injections are given every year. The number of 
injections given to infants (less than one year age) is almost twice as 
compared to older individuals. 
(ii) An average person receives 3-6 injections per year. 
(iii) 74.5% of the injections are administered/given by using plastic 
syringes, the rest being given by using glass syringes. 
(iv) Injections given with glass syringes are more likely to be unsafe as 
compared to those administered with plastic syringes. 
(v) Of the total number of unsafe injections, half of them arise because of 
improper sterilization, the other half owing to wrong injection habits of the 
injections givers. 
In order to ensure injection safety, the injection givers need to be 
constantly trained. This aspect is emphasized in the training programme of 
doctors and ANMs. In order to reduce unsafe injection, the Govenrment has also 
taken a decision to introduce Auto Disable (AD) syringes in all the 
immunization clinics and Central Government hospitals from 2005.

Incentives for Rabi production targets 
*246.    PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA:† 
DR.AKHILESHDAS: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to provide incentives to States for 
meeting Rabi targets; 
(b) if so, the steps being taken and incentives that are being provided to 
States to meet Rabi targets: 
(c) whether any concrete programme of action has been prepared to 
† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Prof. Alka 
Balram Kshatriya. 
28 

[17 December, 2004] RAJYASABHA 
meet the shortage of Kharif production which was affected due to delay in 
monsoon; 
(d) whether despite sluggish Kharif production, foodgrain output in 2004 
has been up; and 
(e) if so, whether Government are confident of meeting foodgrain 
shortage so that the demand of foodgrains by States are fully met? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) In addition to on-going programmes, it has been announced by the 
Government to give incentives in the form of rewards to encourage the States in 
achieving the Rabi production targets. There will be a grant of Rs. 1 crore and one 
silver plaque to the best performing State in each of the identified 5 groups of 
the States. The State could utilize the grant for purchase of equipment to enhance 
efficiency and also give honorarium to the deserving officers/teams/farmers who 
have helped in achieving the targets. 
(c) An intensified Rabi campaign 2004-05 has been launched for 
increasing production. Steps to be taken for enhancing the Rabi production 
like expansion of area under different crops by utilizing Rabi fallows, 
ensuring the availability of inputs, propagation of latest crop production 
technologies, etc. were discussed with States in the National Conference 
on Rabi Campaign held in September, 2004. It was followed by campaigns 
at Zonal level. 
For maximizing Rabi production, the media campaign through video-
audio spots on Doordarshan and All India Radio as well as print media, has 
been intensified all over the country to give tips to the farmers for adoption of 
latest production technologies. Kisan Call Centres are also active for providing 
information on up-tcKJate know how and technology to farmers. 
(d) and (e) Considering the efforts being made by the Government 
and favourable soil moisture and weather conditions so far, it is envisaged 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2004] 
that the additional foodgrains production in the Rabi season would meet the likely 
shortage in the Kharif foodgrains output.

opting to revert to the railways they will be treated as surplus and dealt with as 
per rules. This has been envisaged mainly to ensure that the staff do not get the 
feeling that they have been forced to get absorbed in the IRCTC. The transfer of

Funds for Agricultural Marketing 
1591. DR.AKHILESH DAS: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have launched a scheme to make available funds 
for developing and strengthening agricultural marketing only for such States as 
have made certain policy changes towards reforms; 
(b) if so, the nature and details of the policy changes required for the State 
Governments to qualify for the aid under this scheme; and 
(c) the exten of aid extended there-under to different States, so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTI LAL BHURIA): (a) Yes, Sir. The Government has recently 
approved a Central Sector Scheme titled "Development/Strengthening of 
Agricultural Marketing Infrastructure, Grading and Standardization". Under the 
scheme, credit linked investment subsidy shall be provided on the capital cost 
of general or commodity specific infrast ructure for marketing of agricultural 
commodities and for strengthening and modernization of existing agricultural 
markets, wholesale, rural periodic or in tribal areas. The scheme is linked to 
reforms in State Law dealing with agricultural markets (APMC Act). 
(b) Under the existing APMC Act, State Government alone is 
empowered to initiate the process of se tting up of markets for agricultural 
commodities in notified areas. Processing industry can not buy directly 
from the farmers. The farmer is restricted from entering into direct contract 
with any manufacturer as the produce is required to be canalized through 
regulated markets. These restrictions are acting as a disincentive to farmers, 
trade and industries. The State Govern ments have, therefore, been advised 
to amend the APMC Act to allow direct marketing and contract farming 
and to permit setting up of competitive markets in private and cooperative 
sectors. Assistance under the new Scheme will be provided in those States 
that amend the APMC Act accordingly. 
(c) The Scheme was approved by Government for implementation on 
20.10.2004. All the States have since been requested to inform  as to

notify the reforming States for applicability of the Scheme. Reply from the 
States is awaited. As such, no assistance under the Scheme has been provided

and recommend for this purpose methods of technological upgrading 
of crop husbandry, horticulture, animal husbandry, fisheries (inland 
and marine), agro-forestry and agro-processing and associated 
marketing infrastructure. 
Suggest comprehensive policy reforms designed to enhance investment in agri-

horizontar integration of vertically structured programmes. Also, suggest

for forest conservation; 
(b) if so, salient features thereof;

State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) In pursuance of the 
Supreme Court order dated : 30th October, 2002 in IA No. 566 in Writ 
Petition (Civil) No. 202 of 1995, a Compensatory Afforestation Fund has been 
constituted for the purpose of management of money receivable towards 
compensatory afforestation, net present value and any other money recoverable 
in pursuance of the Supreme Court order in this regard, and in compliance of the 
conditions stipulated by the Central Government while according approval to 
projects for diversion of forest land under Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 for non-
forestry uses of the forest land. 
(b) For the management of compensatory afforestation fund, Central 
Government has also constituted a body to be known as Compensatory 
Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA). The 
CAMPA is custodian of the Compensatory Afforestation Fund. This fund 
constitutes receipt of all monies from user agencies towards compensatory 
afforestation, net present value of forest land, catchment area treatment plan 
and/or of compliance of any other condition stipulated by the Central 
Government while according approval under Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. 
The funds collected by CAMPA are required to be maintained interest bearing 
account and invested in Reserve Bank of India, Nationalized Banks, Post Office, 
Government Securities, Government Bonds and deposits. Compensatory 
Afforestation Fund is required to be utilised as follows: 
(i) The money received for compensatory afforestation is required to be 
used as per the site specific schemes received from the States/Union 
Territories along with the proposals for diversion of forest land under 
the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. 
115 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2004] 
(ii) The money received towards Net Present Value (NPV) is to be used 
for natural assisted regeneration, forest management, protection, 
infrastructure development, wildlife protection and management, 
supply of wood and other forest produce saving devices, and other 
allied activities. 
(iii) Money realized from the user agencies in pursuance of the 
Supreme Court orders or decision taken by the National Board for 
Wildlife involving cases of diversion of forest land in protected areas, is 
required to be put in a corpus and the income is to be used 
exclusively for undertaking protection and conservation activities in 
protected areas of the States/UTs. 
(iv) CAMPA is required to release the funds to the concerned States/ UTs in 
predetermined instalments through the State Level Management 
Committee as per the Annual Plan of Operation finalized by the 
concerned States/UTs. 
(c) and (d) Compesatory Afforestation Fund has not been 
operationalised so far, and therefore, no funds have been released to the 
States/UTs from this fund.

1669. SHRI DATTA MEGHE: Will th e Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a)whether it has come to the notice of Government that during the last 
two months more than 100 children have died of some mysterious disease in 
Saharanpur and neighbouring areas in Uttar Pradesh; 
(b)if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have sent any expert team there to look into it 
and identify the virus that has struck there; 
(d)if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor;

Government to take effective measures to control the disease; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKHSMI): (a) to (f) 
Fever and deaths due to encephalitis in the districts of Saharanpur and 
Baghpat have been reported to the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare 
Govt, of India by the health authorities of Government of Uttar Pradesh. 
In Saharanpur district of Uttar Pradesh, 159 cases amongst children 
including 114 deaths (as on 14th December, 2004) due to encephalitis were 
reported from 25th Sept. 2004. 
In district Baghpat (Block Kshekra), 13 deaths were reported from 28th 
September to 23rd October, 2004. No death has been reported thereafter. 
On the request of the State Govt, a multi-disciplinary Central Team 
comprising experts from Central Govt. Hopital, National Institute of 
Communicable Disease, National Vector  Borne Disease Control Programme, 
National Institute of Virology (Indian Council of Medical Research) 
investigated these cases in Saharanpur and Baghpat districts. 
138 

[17 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
The clinical, epidemiological, entomological and serological 
investigations suggested that the outbreaks were due to acute viral 
encephalitis. 
The primary responsibility of instituting medical care and public health 
measures vests with the State Govt. The Central Govt, extends technical 
support as and when required. Guidelin es on public health measures have 
been sent to district and State health authorities by the Central Govt.

Mobile hospital plan 
1691. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's mobile hospital plan, conceived after Gujarat 
earthquake and super cyclone in Orissa, has not been able to take a concrete 
shape, so far; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to expedite the completion of the plan, 
indicating the budget earmarked and the time limit fixed for the purpose? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) 
Government of India, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is procuring a self 
contained, container based mobile hospital. The Hospital Services Consultancy 
Corporation (India) Ltd. [HSCC(I)], a Government of India Enterprise, the 
procurement consultant, has invited International Competitive Bids. Subject 
to the technical evaluation of the bids conforming to the laid down standards, 
procurement procedures would be initiated by HSCC(I) and commissioning is 
likely to be completed by the end 2005. 
Necessary budget provision has been earmarked in the 10th Plan for this 
project under the Scheme for Health Sector Disaster Preparedness and 
Management.

Vaccine potent in sugarbox/crystals 
1693. SHRIGIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a break through has reportedly been found in 
keeping vaccine potent in sugarbox/crystals; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) to (c) M/s 
Panacea Biotech Limited have entered into an agreement with M/s Cambridge 
Biostability Ltd., U.K., for developing a stable vaccine product based on a new 
technology which mimics a natural phenomenon, wherein some organisms are able 
to survive in dried-up form for hundred of years (anhydrohiosis). In this 
technology water within the cell is replaced with a sugar solution the thickens 
when water is excluded to a point of solidifying as a glass and the organisms 
dries out. Cells are kept in a state of suspended animation until re-hydration 
occurs and (the organism-plant, animal or bacteria) returns to life. The process 
is being applied for first time to vaccines. The vaccine is first spray-dried using 
the sugar syrup to form microscopic glass spheres. The dry vaccine is then 
suspended in an approved inert liquid, which can be injected into muscle where 
bodily fluids reactivates the vaccine. The trial of the vaccine prepared by this 
process is yet to begin.

CALLING ATTENTIONTO MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC IMPORTANCE 
Urgent need for the Central Government to intervene for improving civic 
infrastructure in Mumbai city 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [17 December, 2004] 
SHRISANJAY NIRUPAM (Maharashtra): Sir, I beg to call the attention of the 
Minister of Urban Development on the urgent need for the Central Government to 
intervene for improving civic infrastructure in Mumbai city. 
THE MINISTER OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS AND THE MINISTER OF 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD): Si r, the National 
Common Minimum Programme of the United Progressive Alliance (UPA) 
Government lays emphasis on development and expansion of physical 
infrastructure, particularly, in the areas of roads, highways, ports, power, 
railways, water supply, sewage treatment and sanitation. The UPA Government 
is also committed to a comprehensive programme for urban renewal. In order to 
supplement the efforts of the State Governments/Urban Local Bodies and to 
augment their resources, the Central Government provides assistance to them 
through various programmes/schemes. Further, my Ministry appraises and 
recommends urban infrastructure development projects received from the 
State Governments and Urban Local Bodies for seeking external aid. The 
Ministry of Urban Development has  been implementing the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme of Infrastructure Develo pment in mega cities applicable to 
Mumbai, Bangalore, Kolkata, Chennai and Hyderabad and has been assisting the 
State Government of Maharashtra for development of urban infrastructure of 
Mumbai City as per Plan allocations available under the Scheme. The Scheme 
is funded in the ratio of 25:25 by the Centre and the State Government, and 
remaining 50 per cent is mobilized through institutional finance. Prioritization of 
infrastructure projects to be taken up under the Scheme is decided by the 
State-level Sanctioning Committee. 
[MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, since the inception of the Scheme in 1993-94, a 
total number of 48 projects covering water supply, sanitation, traffic and 
transportation, slum and environmental improvement with a total project cost of Rs! 
1015.95 crores have been taken up in Mumbai City. Central assistance to the 
extent of Rs. 255.99 crores and State share of Rs. 235.83 crores have been 
released so far. A sum of Rs. 252.83 crore has been mobilized through 
institutional finance. An expenditure of Rs. 579.69 crores has been incurred. 
For the current year 2004-05, a Central share of Rs. 53.42 crores has been 
earmarked, but only Rs. 17.78 
232 

[17 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
crore could be actually released for want of Utilization Certificates for 2003-04 and 
availability of matching State share for 2003-04 and 2004-05. 
My Ministry is also assisting the St ate Governments in conducting studies 
on traffic and transportation by providing 40 per cent of the cost. A sum of Rs. 0.57 
crores has already been released to the Government of Maharashtra against the 
total cost of Rs. 6.71 crores for preparation of Mumbai Metro Master Plan and 
Detailed Project Reports of some corridors. 
I would also like to bring to the kind attention of this House through you, Sir, that I 
have attended a detailed presentation made by the Government of Maharashtra 
on December 2,2004 at New Delhi in the presence of the Chief Minister of 
Maharashtra, Central Ministers and Members of Parliament from Maharashtra. 
The presentation primarily focussed on development of Mass Rapid Transit 
System, improvement and expansion of the existing railway network, 
improvement of road network, development of freeways like Eastern Freeway, 
Western Freeway, Mumbai Trans-Harbour Link, Housing and other 
infrastructure projects like upgradation of King Edward Memorial Hospital and 
construction of a second International Airport at Navi-Mumbai. After detailed 
discussions on the presentation, I had suggested that a m eeting of all the 
concerned Ministers and Ministries should be convened soon after the current 
Parliament Session to discuss the proposals made on the presentation. 
Sir, a concerted effort on the part of various Ministries, like Ministries of Urban 
Development & Poverty Alleviation, Railways, Civil Aviation, Finance, and Planning 
Commission, would be required to expl ore the possibilities of extending 
assistance sought by the Government of Maharashtra. Further action on the 
proposals of the Government of Maharashtra would be taken after the proposed 
meeting. 
Mr, Deputy Chairman, Sir, I would like to assure the Members of the House 
that it is the intention of the UPA Government to do its utmost to improve and 
upgrade the infrastructure! facilities in Mumbai. This, of course, requires collective 
effort on the part of the Central Government, the Government of Maharashtra 
and the community as a whole. As I have already stated, we will try to pool 
together the resources of various Ministries 
233 

RAJ YA SABHA [17 December, 2004] 
dealing with urban infrastructure, to extend all possible assistance in achieving this 
objective.

Sir, at the outset, I am thankful to you for having granted me the permission 
to speak on the Bill which is for consideration before the House. I am also 
happy and delighted that during t he consideration of the Bill, at an appropriate 
stage, the hon. Minister, ShriArjun Singhji, for whom I have great regard, is going,

towards the society.! am quite sure that I will have a favourable reply from 
ShriArjun Singhji. Sir, the Bill providing reservation for Scheduled 
Castes/Scheduled Tribes for admission in all courses of study, higher, technical, 
professional, higher learning faculties etc. in all the educational institutions in the 
country to give effect to the Preamble, articles 15j£9(2), 46, 38, 39 and 51 A(j) 
of the Constitution of India and all other  provisions incidental thereto, is for 
consideration before the House. Sir, the Bill provides for resevation for admission 
in all courses of study, higher, technica l, professional, higher learning faculties, 
Stc. in all the educational institutions in the country to give effect to the 
Preamble, articles 15, 29(2), 46, 38, 39 and 51A(j) of the Constitution of India 
and all other provisions incidental thereto. 
Sir, my Bill itself is self-explanatory. I do not want to re-produce all the 
provisos which are part of the Bill, and which I have mentioned in the 
Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill. Sir, the Preamble of the Indian 
Constitution assures equality of opportunity and of status, socioeconomic justice 
to all the citizens of India, and due to practice of untouchability on the 
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes living in the inaccessible scheduled 
areas have been denied education and opportunity to higher education is 
lacking due to proverty and illiteracy. 
I do not think there is a need to repeat what is mentioned in the Statement of 
Objects and Reasons of the Bill and in articles 46,38,51A (j) and 15(4) of the 
Indian Constitution, the contents of wh ich are already mentioned in the Bill, 
because it is known to all of us. So, I need not go into the details regarding these 
articles which are parts of the Indian Constitution. Sir, now the question arises 
as to why this Bill has been introduced in this House and which, with the due 
permission of the Chair, is now before the House for consideration. The reasons, 
Sir, are these. In the Indira Sawhney case, the Supreme Court opined that 
reservation in technical, super-specialities and other advanced and specialised 
courses of study shall not be made for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled 
Tribes, and in Dr. Preeti Srivastava's case, the Supreme Court held that 
reservation in 
272 

[17 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
super-specialities in medical courses of study is not in the national interest and 
cannot be made, and it directed the Medical Council of India to consider 
whether reservation for admission in post-graduation course of study would be 
provided to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes and also in post-
graduation centre. In Chandigarh case, five Judges Bench of the Supreme Court 
held that clubbing of the single posts in post-graduation or in super-specialities 
is illegal. It was also held that relaxation of marks with disparity of 10 marks 
between general and reserved candidates for admission of Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes to the extent of reserved seats as illegal. 
Sir, these are the reasons why I moved the Bill for consideration of the House. 
Sir, I would like to point out before this august House that for ensuring 
educational advancement of these people, we have to observe equality in 
education. Sir, the judgements of vari ous courts need to be reconsidered. I 
personally feel that the judgements of the courts are not in keeping with the spirit 
of the Constitution. May I say, Sir, I am surprised that the judgement did not 
mention any Article of the Constitution to support their views. I don't mean to sound 
harsh, but may I mention that this is the same tendency that Dhronacharya 
adopted, who refused to train Ekalavya in archery. He did not admit him in his 
classes. But Ekalavya, was so inspired that he made an image of his Guru 
Dhronacharya, and tried to learn archery on his own. To everyone's surprise, 
he proved to be the specialist in archery among all the disciples, including Arjun. The 
opportunity was not made available to Ekalavya because of Dhronacharya's 
mentality, but ultimately, Ekalavya proved his merit. The same old tradition and 
tendency to deny opportunities is still being continued, Sir. 
Sir, I may now mention what the factual situation is. The maximum 
reservation for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in admisisons to 
various institutions and classes is to the tune of 22.5 per cent, that is, 15 per cent 
for the Scheduled Castes and 7.5 per cent for the Scheduled Tribes. The 
remaining 77.5 per cent was kept intact; they are open seats for the general 
candidates; we are not touching upon that. We are not against the general 
candidates. We are just trying hard for justice. So, what is wrong, under the 
given circumstances, to make reservations for the Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes to whom, for generations together, the rights were denied, who 
were not brought into the mainstream of the society? So, what is wrong with 
providing 22.5 per cent, out of a

rights merely because we imagine that they may not be able to achieve excellence? It is mere 
imagination, just as Dhronacharya's imagination regarding Ekalavya. Ultimately, 
Dhronacharya was proved wrong. So, this is mere imagination, Sir. 
May I quote Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar, who is called the chief architect of the Indian 
Constitution? He said, "Education is a birthright of every person." The doors of educational 
institutions must be open to every citizen of India. The Indian society, which is based on 
Chaturwamya, had totally banned education to the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled 
Tribes for thousands of years. However, of late, due to the advent of Britishers and certain 
revolutionaries, the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes could receive education 
gradually. After Independence, the Constitution of India has provided that education should 
be imparted to all the children free and compulsory. This provision is not yet implemented. 
Education at all levels and faculties must be universal and cannot be denied to any one. 
However, this is not being done. Therefore, it is wrong to deny the Scheduled  Castes and the 
Scheduled Tribes their legitimate right, and nobody can deny that right under any 
circumstances. As I mentioned earlier, I am not

of reservation for admission in various courses is a very important issue. There is

Sir, I hail from Tamil Nadu which has a history of reservation. The history of reservation in 
Tamil Nadu dates back to the last century. The first Madras Revenue Board Order was 
introduced in the year 1851 and some instructions, by way of a Board Order, were given 
in the year 1851. These are all materials placed before the Mandal Commission for its 
analysis. The Madras Revenue Board had instructed the District Collectors to restrict

the number of entrants in se rvice of certain communities and, particularly, the 
Brahmin communities were restricted because of the prevailing statistics at that time. 
It was found that the male literacy ra te among the Tamil Barhmins, at that 
time, was 73.6 per cent as against the other communities, particularly, 
Vellalars, who are supposed to be the other forward class community. Their 
percentage was only 6.9. The literacy in English among the Tamil Brahmins was

When the Justice Party came to power in the Madras Presidency in 1921, 
they brought the Communal GO and that GO was followed up to 1947. On the 
basis of that Communal GO, out of 12 posts, non-Brahmin Hindus were given 5 
posts, Brahmins were given 2 posts, Muslims were given 2 posts, Anglo-Indians 
and Christians were given 1 post and the depressed classes were given one

Communal GO was challenged in the Madras High Court in the famous Champakam

the Supreme Court and the Supreme Court also held that the Communal GO was 
invalid and, therefore, it was struck down. Thereafter, there was a lot of agitations

Constitutional amendment to article 15, sub-clause (iv) of the Constitution was 
brought in. This is the history. Then successive State Governments in Tamil 
Nadu did not stop with reservations. They continued with reservations. Then 
several ConrHnissioris for Backward Classes were appointed. The first among them

the year 1971, the recommendations of  the Sattanathan Commission were 
implemented in the State of Tamil Nadu; whereby the Scheduled Castes and 
the Scheduled Tribes were given 18 per cent reservation and the Backward 
Classes were given 31 per cent reservation
